case.title: The case: outbound damage at a parcel hub
case.text: A hub ships about 18,400 units a week. Customers complain about crushed parcels, and the damage rate is almost twice what was promised. Follow one improvement project through all five steps, with the same numbers you can load as examples in the tools.

modules.name: Define
modules.goal: Agree what problem you are solving, for whom, how you will measure it and what is out of scope.
ideas: Voice of the customer → CTQ
Start from what the customer notices, then turn it into something you can measure: the Critical to Quality requirement.
SIPOC
One line of boxes: Suppliers, Inputs, Process (five to seven steps), Outputs, Customers. It sets the borders of the project before anyone argues about details.
Problem statement
What, where, since when, how much, and the gap to the target. No cause and no solution yet: those come later, from data.
case: Problem
In weeks 36 to 38, 0.57% of outbound units left the hub damaged (104 of 18,400 in week 38) against 0.30% promised to the customer. Credits cost about €1,150 a week.
CTQ
The parcel arrives undamaged: no crushed, torn or wet outer carton.
Scope
In: from the pick face to handover to the driver. Out: linehaul and supplier packaging.
Target
0.30% or lower by week 46, without longer loading times.
mistakes: Writing the solution into the problem: "we need more training".
A scope so wide that the project never ends.
A problem without a number, so nobody can say when it is solved.
tools: to check whether the number is clear to everyone
at the bottom of this page
checklist: The problem has a number, a time frame and a gap to the target.
The CTQ is written from the customer's side.
Scope in and out is agreed.
A sponsor has signed up to the charter.

quiz.q: Which is the best problem statement?
options: Loaders are careless and need more training.
Damage is too high on the outbound dock.
In weeks 36–38, 0.57% of outbound units were damaged against a 0.30% target, costing about €1,150 a week.
We need a new stacking standard.
quiz.why: It says what, when, how much and the gap, and it does not guess the cause or the solution.

options: Cost to quality
Critical to quality
Control the queue
Check the quantity
quiz.why: A CTQ turns what the customer cares about into a requirement you can measure.

options: Drawing the process at a high level, with its suppliers and customers
Calculating the sigma level
Finding the root cause
Setting control limits
quiz.why: SIPOC sets the borders of the process before the project starts measuring.

modules.name: Measure
modules.goal: Find out how the process performs today, with data you can trust, before you change anything.
ideas: Operational definition
Write exactly what counts, with photos. "Damaged" means different things to different people until it is written down.
Data collection plan
What is recorded, where, by whom, how often and in which format. Record the stage and cause at the moment a problem is found.
Check the measurement
Let two people judge the same twenty cases. If they disagree, fix the definition before you trust the data.
Baseline
The current level as a rate, DPMO and sigma level, over two to four weeks.
case: Definition
A unit is damaged when the outer carton is crushed, torn or wet enough for the customer to notice, found anywhere from the pick face to driver handover.
Check
Two shift leads judged the same 20 cartons and agreed on 17. Three were "slightly dented": the definition got a photo of what counts and what does not.
Baseline
104 damaged of 18,400 units: 0.57%, DPMO 5,652, sigma level 4.03.
mistakes: Changing the process while you are still measuring it.
Trusting a number that two people would count differently.
Measuring only at the end of the line, so you never see where it starts.
tools: to log by stage and cause
checklist: The definition is written, with photos of what counts.
Everyone logs the same way, with stage and cause.
There are at least two weeks of data.
The baseline is written as a rate, DPMO and sigma level.

options: So that different people count the same thing the same way
Because the auditor asks for it
To make the number look better
To shorten the project
quiz.why: Without one, a change in the number can simply mean a change in who is counting.

quiz.q: 104 damaged units out of 18,400, one chance per unit. What is the DPMO?
Two leads judge the same 20 cartons and disagree on five. What comes first?
options: Start improving anyway
Average their answers
Fix the definition and the measurement before trusting the data
Use the stricter lead's answers
quiz.why: A measurement you cannot repeat will hide or invent improvements later.

modules.name: Analyze
modules.goal: Find the few root causes behind most of the problem, and prove them with data rather than opinions.
ideas: Pareto
Sort causes by size. Usually two or three carry about 80% of the problem: the vital few.
Stratify
Split the data by stage, shift, hour, product or route. Problems hide in averages.
Go and see
Watch the work where the number is produced, at the time it goes wrong.
5 Whys and the fishbone
Ask why until you reach something in the process you can change. The fishbone checks people, method, machines, material, measurement and environment.
Common or special cause
A control chart tells you whether you are looking at a normal level of the process or at a few unusual days.
case: Pareto
Stacking 56%, load securing 14%, handling 11%: three causes carry 81% of the damage.
Where and when
63% is found at loading, 60% on the late shift, most of it in the 11:00 departure wave.
On the floor
At the late wave, loaders build walls fast and put heavy parcels on top to fill gaps. There is no stacking rule at the dock.
Proof
Damage per 1,000 units is 2.4 times higher in the peak loading slots than in the others. The control chart shows no special days: the level comes from the method.
mistakes: Stopping at a person: "the loader was careless".
Fixing the loudest complaint instead of the largest bar.
Treating an opinion as a root cause without checking it in the data.
tools: for the Pareto and the stage by type matrix
to reach a cause you can change
to tell common from special causes
checklist: The Pareto shows the vital few.
The top cause was seen on the floor, at the time it happens.
The root cause is in the process, not in a person.
Data confirms it: the cause and the problem move together.

quiz.q: The Pareto shows stacking 56%, load securing 14%, handling 11% and four other causes 19%. Where do you start?
options: With all seven at once
With stacking, then load securing: together 70%
With the smallest, because it is quickest
With handling, because it is about people
quiz.why: The vital few carry most of the problem. Seven small projects at once rarely finish.

quiz.q: Is "the loader was careless" a root cause?
options: Yes, it names who did it
Yes, if it happened twice
Not yet: ask why the process made it possible
No, because loaders are never the cause
quiz.why: People work inside a process. Ask what made the wrong way faster or easier than the right way.

quiz.q: The control chart shows no signals, but the level is too high. What does that mean?
options: The data is wrong
Nothing needs to change
Find the one bad day and fix it
The level comes from the process itself: change the method, do not chase single days
quiz.why: That is common-cause variation. Only a change to the way the work is done moves the level.

modules.name: Improve
modules.goal: Design, test and prove a countermeasure that removes the root cause.
ideas: Options, then choice
Collect several countermeasures and pick by impact and effort. The first idea is rarely the best.
Poka-yoke
Make the error hard to make: layout, markings, fixtures and defaults instead of reminders.
Standard work
Write the new way as a short, visual standard that a new person can follow on day one.
Pilot
Test small, on one dock or one shift, for long enough to see the effect. Plan, do, check, act.
case: Countermeasures

A stacking picture at every dock (heavy low, fragile high, no gaps), floor zones in the vehicle for heavy parcels, load bars after the last wall with a photo, and ten more minutes for the peak loading slots.
Pilot
Docks 3 and 4, two weeks, same definition and same log.
Result
Damage fell from 0.57% to 0.31%. The control chart shows ten days in a row below the old centre line. Loading time rose by two minutes per route: accepted by the sponsor.
mistakes: A reminder at the briefing instead of a change to the work.
Rolling out everywhere before the pilot proves anything.
Ignoring side effects on other numbers, such as loading time.
tools: in Damage Control, to see whether the standard holds
with limits from before the change
checklist: The countermeasure attacks the verified root cause.
It was piloted small before rollout.
Before and after are compared with the same definition.
Side effects on other numbers were checked.

quiz.q: Which countermeasure best prevents heavy parcels ending up on top?
options: Remind loaders at every briefing
A stacking picture and floor zones, so heavy goes low by design
A warning letter after each damage
One more inspection before departure
quiz.why: Reminders fade and inspections find damage after it happens. Design the right way into the work.

options: To learn cheaply and prove the effect before changing everything
Because the sponsor asked for it
To delay the decision
It is not needed when the idea is good
quiz.why: A pilot shows whether the change works, and what else it changes, at low cost.

quiz.q: After the pilot, damage fell but loading time rose six minutes per route. What next?
options: Ignore it: damage was the goal
Stop the project
Look at the side effect and adjust before rolling out
Roll out and hope it settles
quiz.why: A fix that breaks another number will not survive. Adjust, then decide with the sponsor.

modules.name: Control
modules.goal: Keep the gain: make the new way the standard, watch it, and hand it over to the process owner.
modules.output: A control plan and a handover
ideas: Standard and training
Put the new way into the SOP and into onboarding, so it does not depend on the project team.
Control plan
What is measured, how often, by whom, and what to do when a signal appears: the reaction plan.
Control chart
Recalculate the limits from the new stable level and watch for signals, not for single bad days.
Close the project
Hand over to the process owner, record the savings and the lessons, and celebrate the team.
case: Standard
The stacking standard is in the SOP and the onboarding, with the dock pictures.
Control plan
Daily damage on a p-chart with limits from the pilot weeks. A day above the upper limit: the shift lead checks the same shift and runs 5 Whys within 24 hours. A weekly floor check at the dock.
Result
0.31% at 18,400 units a week: about 47 fewer damaged units and €500 less in credits a week. The outbound manager owns it from week 47.
mistakes: Declaring victory when the pilot ends.
Keeping the old limits on the chart, so no signal ever shows.
No owner after the project team leaves.
checklist: The standard is written and trained.
The control chart runs with limits from the new level.
The reaction plan names an owner.
The project is handed over, with savings and lessons recorded.

quiz.q: What must a control plan include?
options: Only the target
What to measure, how often, who, and what to do when a signal appears
The names of the project team
The original problem statement
quiz.why: Without a reaction plan, a signal on the chart is just a red dot nobody acts on.

quiz.q: After the improvement, what happens to the control limits?
options: They stay as they were
They are set to the target
They are recalculated from the new stable period
They are removed
quiz.why: Old limits are too wide for the new process: a relapse would stay inside them unnoticed.

quiz.q: Today is higher than yesterday but inside the limits. What does the reaction plan say?
options: Nothing special: it is noise, keep watching
Call a meeting
Run 5 Whys on the day
Change the standard
quiz.why: Reacting to noise wastes time and can make the process worse. React to signals.

glossary: CTQ
Critical to Quality: a customer need written as something you can measure.
DMAIC
Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control: the five steps of a Six Sigma improvement project.
DPMO
Defects per million opportunities: defects ÷ (units × chances per unit) × 1,000,000.
Sigma level
A way to express how often a process fails. Four sigma is about 6,200 defects per million; six sigma is 3.4.
Yield
The share of units done right the first time.
SIPOC
Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers: a one-line map of a process.
Operational definition
An exact, shared description of what counts, so everyone measures the same way.
Baseline
How the process performs before you change it.
Pareto
Causes sorted by size; the few largest usually carry most of the problem.
Root cause
The cause in the process that, removed, stops the problem coming back.
Common cause
The normal variation built into a process. Only changing the process changes it.
Special cause
Something unusual on a specific day or batch. Find it and remove it.
Control chart
A chart of a measure over time with limits that separate normal noise from real signals.
Poka-yoke
Error-proofing: design that makes the mistake hard or impossible.
Standard work
The current best way to do a job, written short and visual.
Gemba
The place where the work is done. "Go to the gemba": go and see.
Kaizen
Small, continuous improvements made by the people who do the work.
Control plan
What is measured after the project, by whom, how often, and how to react to signals.
wastes: Damaged, incomplete or wrong orders; re-packing and re-delivery.
Picking or packing before the order or the vehicle is ready.
Loaders waiting for the wave, drivers waiting for the load, trucks waiting for a dock.
Loaders who know why damage happens but are never asked.
Moving pallets twice because the staging area is in the wrong place.
Parcels left overnight on the floor; stock that hides counting errors.
Walking to fetch scanners, tape or labels; bending for heavy items stored low.
Scanning the same parcel three times, or double checks nobody reads.
charter: What, where, since when, how much, and the gap to the target
e.g. Parcel arrives undamaged; damaged units ÷ units shipped
e.g. Pick face to driver handover
e.g. About €500 a week in credits
e.g. D wk 39 · M wk 41 · A wk 42 · I wk 45 · C wk 47
